title: “Do Diffusion Models Dream of Electric Planes?” Discrete and Continuous Simulation-Based Inference for Aircraft Design
claim: A complex design is decomposed into a hierarchical tree of discrete choices and continuous parameters, which map to simulated performance outputs and geometry.
layout: 3 panels, left-to-right: tree diagram, numeric output table, CAD render
description: A wide, short figure split into three panels by thin vertical rules, each with a monospace heading. The left panel, 'Aircraft Design Tree', is a hierarchy with 'Aircraft' at the top. Seven branches hang below it: Main Wing(s), Horizontal Tail, Vertical Tail, Fuselage, Battery, Forward Prop. Type and Lift Prop. Type. Main Wing(s) expands to Wing 1, which splits into Lift Rotor Arm and Forward Prop. Arm. The middle panel, 'SUAVE Outputs', is a two-column list of simulator metrics with values: cruise drag, lift, angle of attack, component masses, total mass and battery state of charge. The right panel, 'CAD Visualization', is a grey 3D render of an eVTOL aircraft with blue rotors and red arms. The figure is black on white, with colour only in the render. The eye goes first to the tree.
caption: Summary of the design tree and design parameters, refer to App. [ref], Fig. [ref] for a more detailed image.
abstract: In this paper, we generate conceptual engineering designs of electric vertical take-off and landing (eVTOL) aircraft. We follow the paradigm of simulation-based inference (SBI), whereby we look to learn a posterior distribution over the full eVTOL design space. To learn this distribution, we sample over discrete aircraft configurations (topologies) and their corresponding set of continuous parameters. Therefore, we introduce a hierarchical probabilistic model consisting of two diffusion models. The first model leverages recent work on Riemannian Diffusion Language Modeling (RDLM) and Unified World Models (UWMs) to enable us to sample topologies from a discrete and continuous space. For the second model we introduce a masked diffusion approach to sample the corresponding parameters conditioned on the topology. Our approach rediscovers known trends and governing physical laws in aircraft design, while significantly accelerating design generation.
